materials.rawText:
Projectile Motion
1. Introduction
Projectile motion is the motion of an object that is thrown or projected into the air and then moves
under the effect of gravity.
Examples
A ball thrown into the air
A cricket ball hit by a batsman
A stone thrown at an angle
Water coming out of a fountain
When an object moves as a projectile, its path is usually curved. This curved path is called a trajectory.
2. What Forces Act on a Projectile?
In basic projectile motion, we usually ignore air resistance.
The main force acting on the object is:
Gravity
Gravity pulls the object downward toward the Earth.
Because of gravity:
The vertical velocity changes continuously.
The horizontal velocity remains constant.
The object accelerates downward with acceleration:
g = 9.8 m/s²
For simple numerical problems, we sometimes use:
g = 10 m/s²

3. Types of Projectile Motion
There are two basic types.
A. Horizontal Projectile
In this case, an object is thrown horizontally from a certain height.
Example
Imagine dropping a ball from a table and throwing another ball horizontally from the same table.
Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.
Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity increases downward due to gravity.
B. Projectile Thrown at an Angle
In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.
Example
A football is kicked at an angle of 30°, 45°, or 60°.
The object �rst moves upward, slows down, reaches its highest point, and then falls back down.
4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s
5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t
where:
x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.
6. Vertical Motion
In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.
The vertical velocity after time t is:

vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.
7. Motion at the Highest Point
As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.
So, at the highest point:
Vertical velocity = 0
Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.
8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.
9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m
10. Horizontal Range
The horizontal range is the total horizontal distance travelled by the projectile before it lands.
The formula is:
R = u² sin 2θ / g
where:
R = horizontal range
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
Example
A projectile is launched with:
u = 20 m/s
at:
θ = 30°
Take g = 10 m/s².

R = 20² sin 60° / 10
R = 400(0.866) / 10
R = 34.64 m
Answer: Horizontal range = 34.64 m
11. Important Special Case: 45°
For a given initial velocity, the projectile gets its maximum horizontal range when:
θ = 45°
At this angle:
sin 90° = 1
Therefore:
Rmax = u² / g
Example
If:
u = 20 m/s
and:
g = 10 m/s²
then:
Rmax = 20² / 10
Rmax = 40 m
12. Complete Example
A ball is thrown with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 30°. Take g = 10 m/s².

Find:
�. Horizontal component of velocity
�. Vertical component of velocity
�. Time of �ight
�. Maximum height
�. Horizontal range
Step 1: Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 17.32 m/s
Step 2: Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 10 m/s
Step 3: Time of Flight
T = 2u sin θ / g
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 s
Step 4: Maximum Height
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
H = 5 m
Step 5: Horizontal Range
R = u² sin 2θ / g
R = 400 sin 60° / 10

R = 34.64 m
Final Answers
QuantityAnswer
Horizontal velocity17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity10 m/s
Time of �ight2 s
Maximum height5 m
Horizontal range34.64 m
13. Quick Summary
Projectile motion is the motion of an object thrown into the air under the in�uence of gravity.
The path followed is called a trajectory.
Horizontal motion and vertical motion are treated separately.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity changes because of gravity.
At the highest point, vertical velocity becomes zero.
Time of �ight tells us how long the object stays in the air.
Maximum height tells us how high it goes.
Range tells us how far it travels horizontally.
For the maximum range, the angle of projection is 45°.
Important Formulas
uₓ = u cos θ
uᵧ = u sin θ
T = 2u sin θ / g
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
R = u² sin 2θ / g
These formulas assume that air resistance is ignored and that the projectile lands at the same height
from which it was launched.

materials.rawText:
Projectile Motion
1. Introduction
Projectile motion is the motion of an object that is thrown or projected into the air and then moves
under the effect of gravity.
Examples
A ball thrown into the air
A cricket ball hit by a batsman
A stone thrown at an angle
Water coming out of a fountain
When an object moves as a projectile, its path is usually curved. This curved path is called a trajectory.
2. What Forces Act on a Projectile?
In basic projectile motion, we usually ignore air resistance.
The main force acting on the object is:
Gravity
Gravity pulls the object downward toward the Earth.
Because of gravity:
The vertical velocity changes continuously.
The horizontal velocity remains constant.
The object accelerates downward with acceleration:
g = 9.8 m/s²
For simple numerical problems, we sometimes use:
g = 10 m/s²

3. Types of Projectile Motion
There are two basic types.
A. Horizontal Projectile
In this case, an object is thrown horizontally from a certain height.
Example
Imagine dropping a ball from a table and throwing another ball horizontally from the same table.
Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.
Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity increases downward due to gravity.
B. Projectile Thrown at an Angle
In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.
Example
A football is kicked at an angle of 30°, 45°, or 60°.
The object �rst moves upward, slows down, reaches its highest point, and then falls back down.
4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s
5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t
where:
x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.
6. Vertical Motion
In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.
The vertical velocity after time t is:

vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.
7. Motion at the Highest Point
As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.
So, at the highest point:
Vertical velocity = 0
Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.
8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.
9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m
10. Horizontal Range
The horizontal range is the total horizontal distance travelled by the projectile before it lands.
The formula is:
R = u² sin 2θ / g
where:
R = horizontal range
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
Example
A projectile is launched with:
u = 20 m/s
at:
θ = 30°
Take g = 10 m/s².

R = 20² sin 60° / 10
R = 400(0.866) / 10
R = 34.64 m
Answer: Horizontal range = 34.64 m
11. Important Special Case: 45°
For a given initial velocity, the projectile gets its maximum horizontal range when:
θ = 45°
At this angle:
sin 90° = 1
Therefore:
Rmax = u² / g
Example
If:
u = 20 m/s
and:
g = 10 m/s²
then:
Rmax = 20² / 10
Rmax = 40 m

�. Vertical component of velocity
�. Time of �ight
�. Maximum height
�. Horizontal range

Step 2: Vertical Component

T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10

Step 4: Maximum Height

H = 5 m
Step 5: Horizontal Range

R = 400 sin 60° / 10

Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.

u = 20 m/s

Vertical velocity = 10 m/s

In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

aₓ = 0

u = initial velocity

t = time

a = -g

As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.

vᵧ = 0

u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection

u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:

In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.

4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.

u = 20 m/s

uₓ = 20 cos 30°

Vertical velocity = 10 m/s

In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

aₓ = 0

a = -g

As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.

vᵧ = 0

Horizontal velocity = constant

T = 2u sin θ / g

In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

aₓ = 0

Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:

u sin θ controls the vertical motion.

Vertical velocity = 10 m/s

In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

aₓ = 0

a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.

The vertical displacement is:

As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.

Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.

The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:

u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°

g = 10 m/s²

Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.

Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s

u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s
5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t
where:
x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.
6. Vertical Motion
In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.
The vertical velocity after time t is:

vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.
7. Motion at the Highest Point
As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.
So, at the highest point:
Vertical velocity = 0
Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.
8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.
9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m
10. Horizontal Range
The horizontal range is the total horizontal distance travelled by the projectile before it lands.
The formula is:
R = u² sin 2θ / g
where:
R = horizontal range
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
Example
A projectile is launched with:
u = 20 m/s
at:
θ = 30°
Take g = 10 m/s².

R = 20² sin 60° / 10
R = 400(0.866) / 10
R = 34.64 m
Answer: Horizontal range = 34.64 m
11. Important Special Case: 45°
For a given initial velocity, the projectile gets its maximum horizontal range when:
θ = 45°
At this angle:
sin 90° = 1
Therefore:
Rmax = u² / g
Example
If:
u = 20 m/s
and:
g = 10 m/s²
then:
Rmax = 20² / 10
Rmax = 40 m
12. Complete Example
A ball is thrown with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 30°. Take g = 10 m/s².

Find:
�. Horizontal component of velocity
�. Vertical component of velocity
�. Time of �ight
�. Maximum height
�. Horizontal range
Step 1: Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 17.32 m/s
Step 2: Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 10 m/s
Step 3: Time of Flight
T = 2u sin θ / g
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 s
Step 4: Maximum Height
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
H = 5 m
Step 5: Horizontal Range
R = u² sin 2θ / g
R = 400 sin 60° / 10

R = 34.64 m
Final Answers
QuantityAnswer
Horizontal velocity17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity10 m/s
Time of �ight2 s
Maximum height5 m
Horizontal range34.64 m
13. Quick Summary
Projectile motion is the motion of an object thrown into the air under the in�uence of gravity.
The path followed is called a trajectory.
Horizontal motion and vertical motion are treated separately.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity changes because of gravity.
At the highest point, vertical velocity becomes zero.
Time of �ight tells us how long the object stays in the air.
Maximum height tells us how high it goes.
Range tells us how far it travels horizontally.
For the maximum range, the angle of projection is 45°.
Important Formulas
uₓ = u cos θ
uᵧ = u sin θ
T = 2u sin θ / g
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
R = u² sin 2θ / g
These formulas assume that air resistance is ignored and that the projectile lands at the same height
from which it was launched.

Projectile motion is the motion of an object that is thrown or projected into the air and then moves
under the effect of gravity.
Examples
A ball thrown into the air

A stone thrown at an angle
Water coming out of a fountain
When an object moves as a projectile, its path is usually curved. This curved path is called a trajectory.

3. Types of Projectile Motion
There are two basic types.
A. Horizontal Projectile
In this case, an object is thrown horizontally from a certain height.
Example
Imagine dropping a ball from a table and throwing another ball horizontally from the same table.
Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.
Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity increases downward due to gravity.
B. Projectile Thrown at an Angle
In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.
Example
A football is kicked at an angle of 30°, 45°, or 60°.
The object �rst moves upward, slows down, reaches its highest point, and then falls back down.

materials.rawText:
Projectile Motion
1. Introduction
Projectile motion is the motion of an object that is thrown or projected into the air and then moves
under the effect of gravity.
Examples
A ball thrown into the air
A cricket ball hit by a batsman
A stone thrown at an angle
Water coming out of a fountain
When an object moves as a projectile, its path is usually curved. This curved path is called a trajectory.
2. What Forces Act on a Projectile?
In basic projectile motion, we usually ignore air resistance.
The main force acting on the object is:
Gravity
Gravity pulls the object downward toward the Earth.
Because of gravity:
The vertical velocity changes continuously.
The horizontal velocity remains constant.
The object accelerates downward with acceleration:
g = 9.8 m/s²
For simple numerical problems, we sometimes use:
g = 10 m/s²

3. Types of Projectile Motion
There are two basic types.
A. Horizontal Projectile
In this case, an object is thrown horizontally from a certain height.
Example
Imagine dropping a ball from a table and throwing another ball horizontally from the same table.
Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.
Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity increases downward due to gravity.
B. Projectile Thrown at an Angle
In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.
Example
A football is kicked at an angle of 30°, 45°, or 60°.
The object �rst moves upward, slows down, reaches its highest point, and then falls back down.
4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s
5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t
where:
x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.
6. Vertical Motion
In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.
The vertical velocity after time t is:

vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.
7. Motion at the Highest Point
As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.
So, at the highest point:
Vertical velocity = 0
Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.
8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.
9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m
10. Horizontal Range
The horizontal range is the total horizontal distance travelled by the projectile before it lands.
The formula is:
R = u² sin 2θ / g
where:
R = horizontal range
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
Example
A projectile is launched with:
u = 20 m/s
at:
θ = 30°
Take g = 10 m/s².

R = 20² sin 60° / 10
R = 400(0.866) / 10
R = 34.64 m
Answer: Horizontal range = 34.64 m
11. Important Special Case: 45°
For a given initial velocity, the projectile gets its maximum horizontal range when:
θ = 45°
At this angle:
sin 90° = 1
Therefore:
Rmax = u² / g
Example
If:
u = 20 m/s
and:
g = 10 m/s²
then:
Rmax = 20² / 10
Rmax = 40 m
12. Complete Example
A ball is thrown with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 30°. Take g = 10 m/s².

Find:
�. Horizontal component of velocity
�. Vertical component of velocity
�. Time of �ight
�. Maximum height
�. Horizontal range
Step 1: Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 17.32 m/s
Step 2: Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 10 m/s
Step 3: Time of Flight
T = 2u sin θ / g
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 s
Step 4: Maximum Height
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
H = 5 m
Step 5: Horizontal Range
R = u² sin 2θ / g
R = 400 sin 60° / 10

R = 34.64 m
Final Answers
QuantityAnswer
Horizontal velocity17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity10 m/s
Time of �ight2 s
Maximum height5 m
Horizontal range34.64 m

The path followed is called a trajectory.

Time of �ight tells us how long the object stays in the air.

For the maximum range, the angle of projection is 45°.
Important Formulas

T = 2u sin θ / g

from which it was launched.

materials.rawText:
Projectile Motion
1. Introduction
Projectile motion is the motion of an object that is thrown or projected into the air and then moves
under the effect of gravity.
Examples
A ball thrown into the air
A cricket ball hit by a batsman
A stone thrown at an angle
Water coming out of a fountain
When an object moves as a projectile, its path is usually curved. This curved path is called a trajectory.
2. What Forces Act on a Projectile?
In basic projectile motion, we usually ignore air resistance.
The main force acting on the object is:
Gravity
Gravity pulls the object downward toward the Earth.
Because of gravity:
The vertical velocity changes continuously.
The horizontal velocity remains constant.
The object accelerates downward with acceleration:
g = 9.8 m/s²
For simple numerical problems, we sometimes use:
g = 10 m/s²

3. Types of Projectile Motion
There are two basic types.
A. Horizontal Projectile
In this case, an object is thrown horizontally from a certain height.
Example
Imagine dropping a ball from a table and throwing another ball horizontally from the same table.
Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.
Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity increases downward due to gravity.
B. Projectile Thrown at an Angle
In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.
Example
A football is kicked at an angle of 30°, 45°, or 60°.
The object �rst moves upward, slows down, reaches its highest point, and then falls back down.
4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s
5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t
where:
x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.
6. Vertical Motion
In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.
The vertical velocity after time t is:

vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.
7. Motion at the Highest Point
As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.
So, at the highest point:
Vertical velocity = 0
Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.
8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.
9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m
10. Horizontal Range
The horizontal range is the total horizontal distance travelled by the projectile before it lands.
The formula is:
R = u² sin 2θ / g
where:
R = horizontal range
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
Example
A projectile is launched with:
u = 20 m/s
at:
θ = 30°
Take g = 10 m/s².

R = 20² sin 60° / 10
R = 400(0.866) / 10
R = 34.64 m
Answer: Horizontal range = 34.64 m
11. Important Special Case: 45°
For a given initial velocity, the projectile gets its maximum horizontal range when:
θ = 45°
At this angle:
sin 90° = 1
Therefore:
Rmax = u² / g
Example
If:
u = 20 m/s
and:
g = 10 m/s²
then:
Rmax = 20² / 10
Rmax = 40 m
12. Complete Example

Find:
�. Horizontal component of velocity
�. Vertical component of velocity
�. Time of �ight
�. Maximum height
�. Horizontal range
Step 1: Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 17.32 m/s
Step 2: Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ

uᵧ = 10 m/s
Step 3: Time of Flight
T = 2u sin θ / g
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 s
Step 4: Maximum Height
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
H = 5 m
Step 5: Horizontal Range
R = u² sin 2θ / g
R = 400 sin 60° / 10

R = 34.64 m

There are two basic types.

4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s

5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t

x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.

In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.

The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.

8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.

materials.rawText:
Projectile Motion
1. Introduction
Projectile motion is the motion of an object that is thrown or projected into the air and then moves
under the effect of gravity.
Examples
A ball thrown into the air
A cricket ball hit by a batsman
A stone thrown at an angle
Water coming out of a fountain
When an object moves as a projectile, its path is usually curved. This curved path is called a trajectory.
2. What Forces Act on a Projectile?
In basic projectile motion, we usually ignore air resistance.
The main force acting on the object is:
Gravity
Gravity pulls the object downward toward the Earth.
Because of gravity:
The vertical velocity changes continuously.
The horizontal velocity remains constant.
The object accelerates downward with acceleration:
g = 9.8 m/s²
For simple numerical problems, we sometimes use:
g = 10 m/s²

3. Types of Projectile Motion
There are two basic types.
A. Horizontal Projectile
In this case, an object is thrown horizontally from a certain height.
Example
Imagine dropping a ball from a table and throwing another ball horizontally from the same table.
Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.
Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity increases downward due to gravity.
B. Projectile Thrown at an Angle
In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.
Example
A football is kicked at an angle of 30°, 45°, or 60°.
The object �rst moves upward, slows down, reaches its highest point, and then falls back down.
4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s
5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t
where:
x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.
6. Vertical Motion
In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.
The vertical velocity after time t is:

vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.
7. Motion at the Highest Point
As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.
So, at the highest point:
Vertical velocity = 0
Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.
8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.
9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m
10. Horizontal Range
The horizontal range is the total horizontal distance travelled by the projectile before it lands.
The formula is:
R = u² sin 2θ / g
where:
R = horizontal range
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
Example
A projectile is launched with:
u = 20 m/s
at:
θ = 30°
Take g = 10 m/s².

R = 20² sin 60° / 10
R = 400(0.866) / 10
R = 34.64 m
Answer: Horizontal range = 34.64 m
11. Important Special Case: 45°
For a given initial velocity, the projectile gets its maximum horizontal range when:
θ = 45°
At this angle:
sin 90° = 1
Therefore:
Rmax = u² / g
Example
If:
u = 20 m/s
and:
g = 10 m/s²
then:
Rmax = 20² / 10
Rmax = 40 m
12. Complete Example
A ball is thrown with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 30°. Take g = 10 m/s².

Find:
�. Horizontal component of velocity
�. Vertical component of velocity
�. Time of �ight
�. Maximum height
�. Horizontal range
Step 1: Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 17.32 m/s
Step 2: Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 10 m/s
Step 3: Time of Flight
T = 2u sin θ / g
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 s
Step 4: Maximum Height
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
H = 5 m
Step 5: Horizontal Range
R = u² sin 2θ / g
R = 400 sin 60° / 10

R = 34.64 m
Final Answers
QuantityAnswer
Horizontal velocity17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity10 m/s
Time of �ight2 s
Maximum height5 m
Horizontal range34.64 m
13. Quick Summary
Projectile motion is the motion of an object thrown into the air under the in�uence of gravity.
The path followed is called a trajectory.
Horizontal motion and vertical motion are treated separately.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity changes because of gravity.
At the highest point, vertical velocity becomes zero.
Time of �ight tells us how long the object stays in the air.
Maximum height tells us how high it goes.
Range tells us how far it travels horizontally.
For the maximum range, the angle of projection is 45°.
Important Formulas
uₓ = u cos θ
uᵧ = u sin θ
T = 2u sin θ / g
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
R = u² sin 2θ / g
These formulas assume that air resistance is ignored and that the projectile lands at the same height
from which it was launched.

under the effect of gravity.

materials.rawText:
Projectile Motion
1. Introduction
Projectile motion is the motion of an object that is thrown or projected into the air and then moves
under the effect of gravity.
Examples
A ball thrown into the air
A cricket ball hit by a batsman
A stone thrown at an angle
Water coming out of a fountain
When an object moves as a projectile, its path is usually curved. This curved path is called a trajectory.
2. What Forces Act on a Projectile?
In basic projectile motion, we usually ignore air resistance.
The main force acting on the object is:
Gravity
Gravity pulls the object downward toward the Earth.
Because of gravity:
The vertical velocity changes continuously.
The horizontal velocity remains constant.
The object accelerates downward with acceleration:
g = 9.8 m/s²
For simple numerical problems, we sometimes use:
g = 10 m/s²

3. Types of Projectile Motion
There are two basic types.
A. Horizontal Projectile
In this case, an object is thrown horizontally from a certain height.
Example
Imagine dropping a ball from a table and throwing another ball horizontally from the same table.
Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.
Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity increases downward due to gravity.
B. Projectile Thrown at an Angle
In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.
Example
A football is kicked at an angle of 30°, 45°, or 60°.
The object �rst moves upward, slows down, reaches its highest point, and then falls back down.
4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s
5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t
where:
x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.
6. Vertical Motion
In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.
The vertical velocity after time t is:

vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.
7. Motion at the Highest Point
As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.
So, at the highest point:
Vertical velocity = 0
Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.
8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.
9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m
10. Horizontal Range
The horizontal range is the total horizontal distance travelled by the projectile before it lands.
The formula is:
R = u² sin 2θ / g
where:
R = horizontal range
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
Example
A projectile is launched with:
u = 20 m/s
at:
θ = 30°
Take g = 10 m/s².

R = 20² sin 60° / 10
R = 400(0.866) / 10
R = 34.64 m
Answer: Horizontal range = 34.64 m
11. Important Special Case: 45°
For a given initial velocity, the projectile gets its maximum horizontal range when:
θ = 45°
At this angle:
sin 90° = 1
Therefore:
Rmax = u² / g
Example
If:
u = 20 m/s
and:
g = 10 m/s²
then:
Rmax = 20² / 10
Rmax = 40 m
12. Complete Example
A ball is thrown with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 30°. Take g = 10 m/s².

Find:
�. Horizontal component of velocity
�. Vertical component of velocity
�. Time of �ight
�. Maximum height
�. Horizontal range
Step 1: Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 17.32 m/s
Step 2: Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 10 m/s
Step 3: Time of Flight
T = 2u sin θ / g
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 s
Step 4: Maximum Height
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
H = 5 m
Step 5: Horizontal Range
R = u² sin 2θ / g
R = 400 sin 60° / 10

R = 34.64 m
Final Answers

Vertical velocity10 m/s
Time of �ight2 s
Maximum height5 m
Horizontal range34.64 m

9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m

materials.rawText:
Projectile Motion
1. Introduction
Projectile motion is the motion of an object that is thrown or projected into the air and then moves
under the effect of gravity.
Examples
A ball thrown into the air
A cricket ball hit by a batsman
A stone thrown at an angle
Water coming out of a fountain
When an object moves as a projectile, its path is usually curved. This curved path is called a trajectory.
2. What Forces Act on a Projectile?
In basic projectile motion, we usually ignore air resistance.
The main force acting on the object is:
Gravity
Gravity pulls the object downward toward the Earth.
Because of gravity:
The vertical velocity changes continuously.
The horizontal velocity remains constant.
The object accelerates downward with acceleration:
g = 9.8 m/s²
For simple numerical problems, we sometimes use:
g = 10 m/s²

3. Types of Projectile Motion
There are two basic types.
A. Horizontal Projectile
In this case, an object is thrown horizontally from a certain height.
Example
Imagine dropping a ball from a table and throwing another ball horizontally from the same table.
Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.
Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity increases downward due to gravity.
B. Projectile Thrown at an Angle
In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.
Example
A football is kicked at an angle of 30°, 45°, or 60°.
The object �rst moves upward, slows down, reaches its highest point, and then falls back down.
4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s
5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t
where:
x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.
6. Vertical Motion
In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.
The vertical velocity after time t is:

vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.
7. Motion at the Highest Point
As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.
So, at the highest point:
Vertical velocity = 0
Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.
8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.
9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m
10. Horizontal Range
The horizontal range is the total horizontal distance travelled by the projectile before it lands.
The formula is:
R = u² sin 2θ / g
where:
R = horizontal range
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
Example
A projectile is launched with:
u = 20 m/s
at:
θ = 30°
Take g = 10 m/s².

R = 20² sin 60° / 10
R = 400(0.866) / 10
R = 34.64 m
Answer: Horizontal range = 34.64 m
11. Important Special Case: 45°
For a given initial velocity, the projectile gets its maximum horizontal range when:
θ = 45°
At this angle:
sin 90° = 1
Therefore:
Rmax = u² / g
Example
If:
u = 20 m/s
and:
g = 10 m/s²
then:
Rmax = 20² / 10
Rmax = 40 m
12. Complete Example
A ball is thrown with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 30°. Take g = 10 m/s².

Find:
�. Horizontal component of velocity
�. Vertical component of velocity
�. Time of �ight
�. Maximum height
�. Horizontal range
Step 1: Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 17.32 m/s
Step 2: Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 10 m/s
Step 3: Time of Flight
T = 2u sin θ / g
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 s
Step 4: Maximum Height
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
H = 5 m
Step 5: Horizontal Range
R = u² sin 2θ / g
R = 400 sin 60° / 10

R = 34.64 m
Final Answers

Vertical velocity10 m/s

Horizontal range34.64 m

Projectile Motion
1. Introduction
Projectile motion is the motion of an object that is thrown or projected into the air and then moves
under the effect of gravity.
Examples
A ball thrown into the air
A cricket ball hit by a batsman
A stone thrown at an angle
Water coming out of a fountain
When an object moves as a projectile, its path is usually curved. This curved path is called a trajectory.
2. What Forces Act on a Projectile?
In basic projectile motion, we usually ignore air resistance.
The main force acting on the object is:
Gravity
Gravity pulls the object downward toward the Earth.
Because of gravity:
The vertical velocity changes continuously.
The horizontal velocity remains constant.
The object accelerates downward with acceleration:
g = 9.8 m/s²
For simple numerical problems, we sometimes use:
g = 10 m/s²

3. Types of Projectile Motion
There are two basic types.
A. Horizontal Projectile
In this case, an object is thrown horizontally from a certain height.
Example
Imagine dropping a ball from a table and throwing another ball horizontally from the same table.
Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.
Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity increases downward due to gravity.
B. Projectile Thrown at an Angle
In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.
Example
A football is kicked at an angle of 30°, 45°, or 60°.
The object �rst moves upward, slows down, reaches its highest point, and then falls back down.
4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s
5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t
where:
x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.
6. Vertical Motion
In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.
The vertical velocity after time t is:

vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.
7. Motion at the Highest Point
As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.
So, at the highest point:
Vertical velocity = 0
Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.
8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.
9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m
10. Horizontal Range
The horizontal range is the total horizontal distance travelled by the projectile before it lands.
The formula is:
R = u² sin 2θ / g
where:
R = horizontal range
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
Example
A projectile is launched with:
u = 20 m/s
at:
θ = 30°
Take g = 10 m/s².

R = 20² sin 60° / 10
R = 400(0.866) / 10
R = 34.64 m
Answer: Horizontal range = 34.64 m
11. Important Special Case: 45°

θ = 45°
At this angle:
sin 90° = 1
Therefore:
Rmax = u² / g
Example

u = 20 m/s
and:
g = 10 m/s²
then:
Rmax = 20² / 10
Rmax = 40 m

In basic projectile motion, we usually ignore air resistance.
The main force acting on the object is:
Gravity
Gravity pulls the object downward toward the Earth.
Because of gravity:
The vertical velocity changes continuously.
The horizontal velocity remains constant.
The object accelerates downward with acceleration:
g = 9.8 m/s²
For simple numerical problems, we sometimes use:
g = 10 m/s²

chunks.text:
3. Types of Projectile Motion
There are two basic types.
A. Horizontal Projectile
In this case, an object is thrown horizontally from a certain height.
Example
Imagine dropping a ball from a table and throwing another ball horizontally from the same table.
Both balls fall downward because of gravity, but the thrown ball also moves forward.
Important Points
Initial horizontal velocity is present.
Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Horizontal velocity remains constant.
Vertical velocity increases downward due to gravity.
B. Projectile Thrown at an Angle
In this case, an object is thrown at an angle with the horizontal.
Example
A football is kicked at an angle of 30°, 45°, or 60°.
The object �rst moves upward, slows down, reaches its highest point, and then falls back down.

chunks.text:
4. Resolving Velocity into Components
Suppose an object is projected with initial velocity u at an angle θ.
We divide this velocity into two parts:

Horizontal Component
uₓ = u cos θ
Vertical Component
uᵧ = u sin θ
So:
u cos θ controls the horizontal motion.
u sin θ controls the vertical motion.
Example
A ball is thrown with velocity:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle:
θ = 30°
Horizontal component:
uₓ = 20 cos 30°
uₓ = 20(0.866) = 17.32 m/s
Vertical component:
uᵧ = 20 sin 30°
uᵧ = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s
Therefore:
Horizontal velocity = 17.32 m/s
Vertical velocity = 10 m/s

5. Horizontal Motion
In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically downward.

Therefore, in the horizontal direction:
aₓ = 0
Since acceleration is zero, horizontal velocity remains constant.
The horizontal distance travelled is:
x = u cos θ × t
where:
x = horizontal distance
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
t = time
Example
A ball is projected with:
u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°
Find the horizontal distance travelled in 2 seconds.
x = u cos θ × t
x = 20(0.866)(2)
x = 34.64 m
Answer: The ball travels 34.64 m horizontally.

6. Vertical Motion
In the vertical direction, gravity acts downward.
The acceleration is:
a = -g
The negative sign means gravity acts downward if upward is considered positive.
The vertical velocity after time t is:

vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
The vertical displacement is:
y = u sin θ × t - ½gt²
These equations help us understand how high the projectile goes and how its vertical velocity changes.

As the projectile moves upward, gravity continuously reduces its vertical velocity.
At the highest point:
vᵧ = 0
This does not mean the object stops completely.
The horizontal velocity is still present.
So, at the highest point:
Vertical velocity = 0
Horizontal velocity = constant
Acceleration = g downward
After reaching the highest point, the projectile starts falling downward.

chunks.text:
8. Time of Flight
The time of �ight is the total time the projectile remains in the air.
For an object projected and landing at the same level, the formula is:
T = 2u sin θ / g
where:
T = total time of �ight
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity

Example
A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take:
g = 10 m/s²
Then:
T = 2(20) sin 30° / 10
Since:
sin 30° = 0.5
T = 2(20)(0.5) / 10
T = 2 seconds
Answer: The ball remains in the air for 2 seconds.

9. Maximum Height
The maximum height is the highest vertical position reached by the projectile.
The formula is:
H = u² sin² θ / 2g
where:
H = maximum height
u = initial velocity
θ = angle of projection
g = acceleration due to gravity
Example

A ball is thrown with:
u = 20 m/s
at an angle of:
30°
Take g = 10 m/s².
H = 20² sin² 30° / 2(10)
H = 400(0.5)² / 20
H = 400(0.25) / 20
H = 5 m
Answer: Maximum height = 5 m

Projectile motion is the motion of an object thrown into the air under the in�uence of gravity.

Vertical velocity changes because of gravity.
At the highest point, vertical velocity becomes zero.
Time of �ight tells us how long the object stays in the air.

uᵧ = u sin θ
